newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss start refurbishing image with Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss start refurbishing image with Holocaust fund.

text.p: Switzerland took a first step to repairing its tarnished reputation by agreeing on Wednesday to set up a Holocaust fund after months of attacks led by Jewish groups over its World War Two financial role, critics said.

"This is really only the beginning," said Maram Stern, assistant secretary general of the World Jewish Congress (WJC), which first put the Swiss in the world spotlight by accusing its secretive banks of hoarding accounts left by Holocaust victims.

"This is a gesture of goodwill on the Swiss side, a small gesture, to start on the process so that the few people who are still alive from the Holocaust should get something back," Stern told Reuters.

Stern said the cabinet's agreement on Wednesday to set up an aid fund for Holocaust survivors must be matched by persistance in carrying out a bank probe and historical inquiry launched in the past nine months.

Swiss banks deny they deliberately kept heirs away from money left by Holocaust victims, but agreed with the WJC last May to a probe by an independent panel with unprecedented powers to lift bank secrecy in order to search historical records.

Then Berne late last year bowed to a drumbeat of attacks from the WJC and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato and named a panel of Swiss and international historians to carry out a sweeping review of Swiss financial relations with Nazi Germany and the flow of stolen wartime assets through its banks.
But both probes will take more time than many ageing Holocaust victims have, prompting the WJC to call for a quick financial gesture -- which the banks and Berne refused until recently.

At the core of both probes were claims that Swiss banks and Swiss authorities, rather than being the innocent neutrals they had made themselves out to be, profited from the Holocaust and aided Hitler's war with financial and economic collaboration.

"Switzerland has a reputation as a long-term, legally safe and customer-friendly financial centre to defend," the president of the Swiss Bankers Association, Georg Kreyer, told reporters only hours before the Holocuast fund was decided.

The danger for Switzerland's reputation peaked in January when world Jewish groups threatened to call a boycott of Swiss banks after outgoing Swiss president Jean-Pascal Delamuraz liked Jewish calls for compensation to "extortion and blackmail".

Delamuraz apologised two weeks later but the country's three biggest banks, embarrased by revelations that UBS had shredded historic documents, feared further controversy and pledged 100 million Swiss francs for a Holocaust fund.

With the cabinet agreement to administer the fund together with the World Jewish Restitution Organistaion (WJRO), both sides can now open a period of "cooperation instead of confrontation" that they agreed to seek at a New York meeting on February 14.
"We are gradually learning how to deal with this (Holocaust issue) and are beginning to think beyond this issue into the future," banker Krayer said.
